lead: On the memorial of St Ambrose, Paul writes from prison to tell Timothy not to be ashamed and to guard what has been entrusted to him. Jesus, on the night before his death, tells disciples who are about to run away that he has conquered the world. Courage in both readings comes from knowing whom we have trusted, not from any strength of our own.

set: This letter presents Paul in chains and near the end of his life: “the time of my departure has come” (4:6). Timothy seems young and easily discouraged, which is why Paul has just reminded him that “God did not give us a spirit of cowardice” (1:7). What will happen to the Gospel when the apostle is gone? The passage answers: it is God's work, and it has been entrusted to faithful hands.
str: v. 8: do not be ashamed; share in suffering.
vv. 9–10: the reason: a short summary of the Gospel, from before the ages to the appearing of Christ.
vv. 11–12: Paul's own example: “I am not ashamed”.
vv. 13–14: hold the pattern, guard the treasure.
kw: what is entrusted, the good treasure (vv. 12, 14)
A legal word for something left in another's safekeeping, to be returned intact. It appears in vv. 12 and 14 and in 1 Timothy 6:20. The Church's phrase “the deposit of faith” comes from here.
A word used for a god or a ruler showing himself. Here it means Christ's coming in the flesh. The letters to Timothy also use it for his return (2 Timothy 4:1).
An outline or model for copying. Timothy does not make up the teaching; he holds to the pattern he received.
vv: who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace.
This grace was given “before the ages began”. Before Timothy was afraid, and before the first prison, God had already acted.
who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.
“Abolished”: made powerless. Death still comes, but it no longer has the last word. A prisoner writing with death ahead of him is the one who says so.
But I am not ashamed, for I know the one in whom I have put my trust, and I am sure that he is able to guard until that day what I have entrusted to him.

Not “I know what” but “I know the one”: faith is first of all trust in a person. The Greek says “my deposit”, which can mean what Paul has entrusted to God (NRSV) or what God has entrusted to Paul (the way the POC takes it).
Guard the good treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit living in us.
Keeping the faith is not only a human effort. The Spirit is the true guardian, and Timothy works with him.
ch: The Catechism says that the apostles entrusted the “sacred deposit” of the faith, contained in Scripture and Tradition, to the whole Church, and cites this passage (CCC 84). St Ambrose, Bishop of Milan from 374, is an example of such guarding. He held firm against the Arian party, even when pressed by the imperial court, and at Easter in 387 he baptized Augustine, who would hand the faith on to many generations.

r.h: Take courage; I have conquered the world
set: These are the last words of the Farewell Discourse (John 13–16), spoken at the table on the night before the Passion. After this comes only the prayer of Jesus to the Father (John 17), and then the arrest. The disciples think that at last they understand. Jesus knows that within hours they will scatter.
str: vv. 25–28: from figures to plain speech: the Father himself loves you. Jesus came from the Father and returns to him.
vv. 31–32: “Do you now believe?” They will scatter, but he is not alone.
kw: Open, unhindered speech. It is also the confidence of those who may speak openly to God (Hebrews 4:16).
Literally “pressure, crushing”: the NRSV has “persecution”, the POC ഞെരുക്കം. Jesus promises it. He does not promise his followers an easy road.
A Greek perfect tense: a victory already won, whose effects last. He says it before the Cross. See 1 John 5:4: “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith”.
vv: for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.
This is the “plain speech” about the Father. Jesus does not stand between us and an unwilling God. The Father himself loves.
The hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each one to his home, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone because the Father is with me.

He says this without any bitterness, naming the coming failure so that it will not destroy them afterward. The cry of Psalm 22 from the Cross (Mark 15:34) must be read together with this confidence: that psalm itself ends in trust.
I have said this to you, so that in me you may have peace. In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!”
“In me” and “in the world” are the two places where a disciple lives at once. Peace does not mean that the trouble is gone; it means that the trouble has been defeated.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 33 when it teaches about the virtue of fortitude, which enables us to conquer fear, even fear of death (CCC 1808). On prayer “in my name” (v. 26), it teaches that faith in the Son brings the disciples into the knowledge of the Father (CCC 2614). When St Ambrose faced pressure in Milan, he and his people kept watch in the church; St Augustine records that it was then that hymns and psalms began to be sung there after the manner of the Eastern regions (in substance, Confessions, Book 9).

qa: Jesus says “I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf” (16:26). Doesn't he intercede for us?

He does: he “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25). In John 16 he is not denying this. He is saying that the disciples are not kept at a distance from the Father, as though only Jesus could speak to him. United with the Son, they themselves can go to the Father, who already loves them.
rite: St Ambrose (died 397) belongs to the Latin West, yet he read and drew on the Greek Fathers of the East. He is a reminder that East and West share one inheritance of faith. As a bishop who stood firm and also taught the newly baptized about the sacraments, he speaks to a Malankara Church in the middle of its fast: guard what you have received, and hand it on to the next generation in your homes and Sunday schools.
study: “I know the one in whom I have put my trust.” What do I need to entrust to him today?
Jesus promises peace in the middle of trouble, not after it. Where can I claim this promise this week?
